stages.title: Vertical and horizontal integration: drawbacks and demergers
stages.sub: The student can explain why integration can backfire and why some firms choose to split apart.

steps.q: A drinks firm buys its glass-bottle supplier, adding a whole new stage of production to manage. As layers of management pile up to coordinate both businesses, does decision-making tend to get quicker or slower?
steps.right: Slower and more costly per unit
steps.hint: Think about what diseconomies of scale do to costs as a firm grows and gets harder to manage.

steps.q: That same drinks firm now owns its bottle supplier, so rival drinks firms struggle to buy bottles from anyone else. Would a competition regulator be likely to take an interest in this?
steps.right: Yes, it may investigate reduced competition
steps.wrong: No, regulators only look at mergers between direct rivals
steps.hint: The regulator's job is to protect competition in the market, not just to watch head-to-head rivals.

steps.q: Two supermarket chains merge into one much larger supermarket business. As head office tries to run twice as many stores and staff, do costs per store tend to fall smoothly or start creeping up?
steps.hint: Bigger is not always better managed. What happens once a business becomes hard to coordinate?

steps.q: One supermarket chain has a relaxed, informal way of working. The chain it merges with is strict and hierarchical. When staff from both suddenly have to work together, is friction likely?
steps.right: Yes, their different ways of working may clash
steps.wrong: No, staff will automatically adopt one style smoothly
steps.hint: Think about two very different workplace habits being forced together overnight.

steps.q: A large conglomerate finds its many divisions are costly to manage together and decides to split off and sell one division as a separate, independent company. What has it just done?
steps.right: Broken the firm into separate parts
steps.wrong: Merged with another firm to add scale
steps.hint: This is the opposite of integrating: the firm is becoming smaller and simpler, not bigger.
